abstract: Mitophagy, the selective autophagic clearance of damaged mitochondria, is tightly governed by the PINK1-Parkin signaling axis. Although the activation of Parkin, driven by phosphorylation of ubiquitin (Ub) and Parkin, has been well characterized, the mechanisms that terminate mitophagy remain poorly understood. Here, we identify the heterotrimeric protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) holoenzyme assembled with the B55 regulatory subunit (PP2A-B55 as the terminator of mitophagy. We demonstrate that PP2A-B55 preferentially dephosphorylates pParkin over pUb in cells, effectively blocking Parkin mitochondrial translocation. Mechanistically, B55 binds Parkin through an interface distinct from the one commonly used to engage PP2A substrates containing disordered short linear motifs (SLiMs), thereby accommodating the folded Parkin ubiquitin-like (Ubl) domain. Leveraging this recognition mechanism, we rationally designed a Parkin-derived competitive inhibitor that validates this non-canonical interface and selectively uncouples pParkin dephosphorylation from the global pUb pool. Together, our findings define a negative regulatory mechanism governing Parkin and provide a proof-of-concept strategy to selectively enhance mitophagy without disrupting broader Ub signaling.
